shared_text:
The flight. An airliner on a passenger flight to an airport in mountainous terrain, in daylight and visual conditions.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring.

What happened. After runway and approach changes and a hold, ATC vectored the aircraft to the approach with a turn of more than 90 degrees; it overshot the inbound course and S-turned onto final. At 1,000 ft the approach was stable: configured, on path, on the 152-knot target speed, runway in sight. At about 500 ft the airspeed rose about 15 knots. The captain reduced power; the speed stayed at 160 knots and the PAPI showed slightly high. Lowering the nose brought a "Sink rate" warning; the captain corrected, reduced power again and lowered the nose slightly, and a second warning sounded. Holding power, in case the added headwind was lost, the captain raised the nose and moved the aim point to 1,500 ft. The manual required a go-around for a sink-rate warning at or below 500 ft unless, in visual conditions, the captain judged the deviation was being corrected immediately and safely. The captain judged that it was, and that the approach was still stable. The captain knew the runway's initial downslope would partly offset the higher descent rate, and saw risk in a go-around in mountainous terrain, with a controller who seemed to be having difficulty managing arrivals. Judging it safer to continue to a controlled touchdown-zone landing, the captain continued.
safe_outcome: The aircraft touched down about 2,500 ft along the runway, and the rollout and taxi were uneventful. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: The aircraft could not be stopped on the remaining runway. It left the end of the runway at about 30 knots and came to rest on the grass. The passengers were evacuated, and two received minor injuries during the evacuation. The aircraft was slightly damaged.
notes: Rule 3 removed: "the vectors complicated the approach unnecessarily" (replaced by the observable overshoot and S-turn). Kept as reasons the captain gave for continuing: the company manual's exception for visual conditions, the captain's judgement that the corrections were immediate and safe and the approach still within stable criteria, the runway's initial downslope, the risk of a go-around in mountainous terrain, and the captain's view of the approach controller (attributed as "seemed to be"). Rule 5 moved to the safe ending: the touchdown at about 2,500 ft and the uneventful rollout and taxi. Omitted for length: the original ILS briefing for the opposite runway, the ATIS details (light wind, broken cloud at 1,800 ft, towering cumulus), the controller declining the RNP approach because of traffic, the two aircraft holding below, the holding fuel and diversion planning, notifying dispatch, cabin crew and passengers, and the partial box pattern of vectors. Judgement calls: the report gives no aircraft type, so the class is "an airliner"; the one-red PAPI is written as "showed slightly high"; the captain's "within stable approach criteria" is kept as the captain's judgement, not as a checked fact.
